item.title: Nvidia CEO called in by lawmakers over ties to alleged Chinese spy
item.description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been asked by three House Republican committee chairs to brief Congress behind closed doors about his reported ties to a woman accused of spying for China.

Why it matters: The request escalates the scrutiny of the Nvidia CEO over his alleged relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman accused of spying for China.

Catch up quick: Jensen Huang and Alice Huang purportedly had a "close" relationship, per reporting from The New York Times.

  • The Times also reported that President Trump was briefed by intelligence officials about their relationship and the allegations that Alice Huang was a spy, but chose not to act.
  • The Wall Street Journal subsequently reported that officials in at least three countries had concerns that Alice Huang was passing information to the Chinese government, potentially including sensitive details on Nvidia chips.
  • Nvidia has denied the allegations, saying Jensen Huang and Alice Huang's contacts were just routine business interactions. The Chinese government previously called the allegations it was spying on Nvidia "groundless speculation."

Zoom out: Reps. Brian J. Mast (R-Fla.), John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) sent a letter to Jensen Huang Thursday, requesting he sit for a joint briefing with the respective House committees that they chair: Foreign Affairs, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the Select Committee on Intelligence.

  • They are seeking answers on Nvidia's protocols to protect itself from foreign adversaries and his interactions with Alice Huang, according to the letter.
  • "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People's Republic of China] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the letter reads.
  • "The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk," the letter continues.

The other side: "Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," Nvidia said in a statement.

  • "Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security," the company said.
  • "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," it added.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with a statement from Nvidia.

item.title: Democrats' big win clouds the permitting picture
item.description:
Democrats' blowout win further complicates the fraught path to passing a permitting deal in the lame duck.

Why it matters: Cutting hurdles for projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors.

  • But critics argue the Senate plan unacceptably weakens environmental protections and tribal input.

The big picture: Dems' looming control of Congress "worsens the outlook" for the bill this year, the advisory firm Capstone said in a note.

  • The firm sees Democrats as "further emboldened" to punt the bill into 2027.
  • President "Trump is likely to put pressure on House Republicans to support the package, but with his standing diminished in the wake of the midterms, his political capital may be limited," it states.
  • Analysts with Jefferies also see reduced odds of lame duck support for a package that makes it easier to build gas pipelines.

Yes, but: The bipartisan bill's Democratic co-authors argued on Wednesday that now remains the time, with Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) calling it a "bird in the hand" and saying "we'd be fools not to take it."

  • "Democrats ran and won on affordability, and this bill lowers costs for families and will allow us to start delivering on our election promises," he said in a statement.

State of play: Rapidan Energy Group now sees a 20%-25% chance in the lame duck, down from 30% pre-election.

  • Yet Rapidan's rather bullish on a permitting deal with Trump in 2027-2028. That challenges the view of many bill supporters who see a fleeting opening right now.
  • Rapidan's logic: Trump struck first-term deals with Dems on the debt limit, government funding and more — at times against the will of GOP congressional leaders.

"Democrats need only five or six Republican votes to reach 60 on a bill Republicans helped write, and Trump's first-term precedent ... suggests he may be willing to make deals with Democrats to reduce the veto risk," their note states.

Catch up quick: TD Cowen analysts quickly dropped their assessment of lame duck passage from 40% to 25%, while the firm ClearView Energy Partners also argues that Dems' bicameral win could weaken the prospects.

What they're saying: American Clean Power Association head Jason Grumet told reporters on Wednesday the bill reflects voters' interest in cheaper energy.

  • "I think that the understanding in Congress is that this is a really unique opportunity, and if you don't move forward in the next three or four weeks, it's hard to imagine a bipartisan effort over the next couple of years," said Grumet, whose group represents renewables, storage and transmission companies.

The other side: Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), who is likely to helm the Natural Resources Committee, is arguing that Democrats should show that the days of Trump's "supplicant Senate" are over. Huffman, who wants to wait until next year, said Dems should demand hearings and amendments on the bill he currently opposes.

The bottom line: The White House is still pushing for lame duck action, but did not directly say whether it would be open to a deal on an altered bill next year.

  • "The White House supports the bipartisan deal worked out between Republicans and Democrats and agrees that the time to get permitting reform done is now," a White House official said.

Amy Harder contributed reporting.

item.title: Tech giants turn to cash, concessions for AI rebrand after voters pummeled data centers 43-1
item.description:
The AI industry is scrambling to repackage a $10 trillion infrastructure buildout to appease a hostile electorate that overwhelmingly voted to restrict data center construction in ballot measures across the country.

  • It's not just changing the name of data centers to "compute campuses," but offering communities real money, including dividends, benefits for schools or cities, environmental concessions and labor protections.

Why it matters: Tuesday's election proved voters won't tolerate unchecked growth, although the market and many analysts see the blue wave slowing — but not stopping — data center construction around the U.S. To prevent an existential threat, the world's biggest companies are working on a rebrand.

  • How well they execute on their promises will determine the pace of the global AI race.

What they're saying: Chris Lehane, OpenAI's chief global affairs officer, compared the turnaround AI must make to the 1996 election, which came shortly after Republicans routed Democrats in a historic midterm election.

  • "A lot happens in two years," he told Axios in an interview. "Smart, talented folks take messages from voters and react and respond to them."
  • Getting community buy-in for data centers will require "really making clear that these can be long-term, durable, economically transformative projects for communities," he said.

Driving the news: There's no question about how voters feel about data centers after Election Day, with restrictive measures across 10 states going 43-1 at the ballot box. The margins weren't close, with an average of 75% of people favoring restrictions.

  • In Texas, a new Democratic governor has promised to keep a moratorium in place until the legislature passes comprehensive reforms.
  • Candidates who won in other emerging data center states also favor similar restrictions. Analysts say about 60% of planned 2028 capacity across the U.S. faces a risk of delay.

Between the lines: Incoming Democrats aren't going to kill data centers. Virginia, run entirely by Democrats, is the biggest data center hub in the U.S. Unions are also among the buildout's biggest supporters. But many of the new crop of winning candidates have similar demands.

  • Tech companies must pay for infrastructure and bring their own power, ensuring that new strains on the grid from the boom won't hit ratepayers.
  • Tax breaks are dead and face repeal, and the companies will have to show that they will ensure environmental and labor protections. Voters also won't tolerate any more nondisclosure agreements or what look like secret deals.

What we're watching: Amazon, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and other major data center developers began laying out a new vision for winning public approval before Tuesday's "AI earthquake."

  • Many of their proposals already include efforts to meet these demands, including commitments to ensure data center developers cover their infrastructure and power costs.
  • These concessions may make data centers more costly, but a slower pace could also make it easier to absorb higher costs.

Zoom in: Jobs won't be enough, since they are temporary. Look for more payments akin to the $50,000 teacher bonuses that followed the construction of a massive Meta data center in Louisiana.

  • Amazon allocated $1 billion for investing in data center communities over five years, and Microsoft also has its "Datacenter Community Pledge."
  • OpenAI on Thursday unveiled a "Compute Campus Policy Blueprint" and outlined tens of millions of dollars of commitments for free school lunches, parks, first responders and other priorities.
  • Lehane added that renaming data centers to compute campuses—viewed as a gimmick by some policymakers and consumer advocates—was an intentional effort to "provoke that conversation."

Yes, but: It's far from clear whether Democrats who are poised to take control of powerful congressional committees in Washington will buy the talking points, and some new state leaders campaigned on the importance of binding agreements.

  • A report last month from Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) found that major tech companies aren't covering the full infrastructure costs of their data centers, and companies continue seeking billions in tax breaks as well as using nondisclosure agreements.

The bottom line: Data center construction is set to slow, but it won't stop. The race is on to see whether Democrats can translate election momentum into binding restrictions or if the industry tries to head off tougher rules.

item.title: Oil prices plunge after Vance post on Iran war
item.description:
Data: Financial Modeling Prep; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios

Oil prices fell sharply Wednesday as traders weigh signs — including a widely circulated post by Vice President JD Vance — that the midterm election will add pressure on the White House to find an offramp from the Iran conflict.

Why it matters: Elections have consequences.

  • Wednesday's price drop — around $8 per barrel — deepened after Vance posted on X that "everyone knows" the war is why Republicans got pummeled and "any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
  • Sen. Chuck Schumer (D), the likely Senate majority leader in the next Congress, vowed that Democrats will push to end the war.

"This crude price drop is entirely about the U.S. election and the belief that Trump will de-escalate rather than escalate on Iran. JD Vance's statement amplified that sentiment," Ben Cahill, a nonresident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council, told Axios via email.

What they're saying: Pavel Molchanov, an analyst with Raymond James, said in remarks circulated to reporters that Vance's post was a "key catalyst" for today's oil price plunge.

  • "The market is saying that Congress and members of his own administration are likely to start acting as a constraint on President Trump's war in Iran," Seb Barker, a strategist with the hedge fund, Marshall Wace, tells the Financial Times.

Catch up quick: Oil prices were already falling to start the week on signs of new U.S.-Iran diplomacy.

What we're watching: "[I]t remains unclear whether Vance's comments signal a more dovish stance toward Iran," Molchanov said.

  • "For oil prices to sustainably move lower, a durable off-ramp is needed," he added.

item.title: Trump can't pack the Fed board with allies now
item.description:
A recurring subplot of President Trump's term has been a desire to replace Biden appointees to the powerful Federal Reserve Board of Governors — even ahead of their terms ending — with allies. That effort now looks dead in the water.

Why it matters: Even if Trump succeeds in his efforts to fire governor Lisa Cook, or to oust any of the other three Biden-era holdovers on the seven-member board, a Democratic Senate will likely block any replacements it views as insufficiently independent from the administration.

State of play: The president seeks to fire Cook — whose term runs through 2038 — for alleged mortgage fraud, an effort that has been blocked so far by the courts. The White House plans a hearing over the allegations next month.

  • Former chair Jerome Powell has remained on the board as a governor, a term that ends in January 2028.
  • Michael Barr, whom former President Biden appointed as top financial regulator, has remained in place as a governor in a term that extends to 2032.
  • Philip Jefferson's term as vice chair ends this coming September, though his term as a governor extends to 2036.

Between the lines: It would break with current precedent for those officials to stick around to the end of their terms. In recent decades, Fed governor spots have turned over much more regularly, particularly after their time as chair or vice chair ends.

  • Powell, Barr and Jefferson may feel greater comfort relinquishing their roles as governors before the end of their terms if they are confident the Senate will block any replacements who don't respect the tradition of central bank independence.

Of note: Sen. Elizabeth Warren is set to chair the Senate Banking Committee that must advance Fed governor nominees, and she has assailed chairman Kevin Warsh for being a "sock puppet" of the administration.

  • Only one Senate Democrat, John Fetterman, voted to confirm Warsh.

item.title: "What we just witnessed was an AI earthquake": Voters revolt against tech at polls
item.description:
Voters showed deep distrust of the AI race Tuesday, approving dozens of data center moratoriums and electing a raft of candidates who favor slowing a $10 trillion buildout, including in Texas — the epicenter of the boom.

Why it matters: In an election that hinged on an affordability crisis for many Americans, voters made it clear they view Silicon Valley's AI ambitions not as a technological miracle, but as a resource-draining threat to their wallets and communities.

  • The results were a warning shot to some of the nation's wealthiest and most powerful executives, many of whom are already working on ways to build a more palatable version of the revolution they are dead set on winning.

"What we just witnessed was an AI earthquake," Brad Carson, co-founder of Americans for Responsible Innovation, told Axios. "Voters just sent a clear message that they want rules for AI and data centers."

Driving the news: Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa's surprise victory in the Texas governor's race fundamentally scrambles the math for the AI buildout.

  • Hinojosa campaigned on keeping a moratorium on data center construction in place until the state passes legislation tackling impacts on water, electricity, air and property rights in the legislative session that ends in mid-2027.
  • While most U.S. data centers expected in 2027 are already under construction, a hold for more than six months would bring extended delays in Texas, which accounts for 41% of new U.S. capacity in 2028, according to the research firm SemiAnalysis.
  • Democrats won all three of the states that follow Texas for new data center capacity, including Ohio, Georgia and Arizona. The winners in Ohio and Georgia favor restrictive policies, although it's not yet clear how those will take shape.

Between the lines: All told, nearly two-thirds of 2028 data center capacity could face delays, although most political analysts don't see Democrats permanently blocking construction.

What they're saying: A host of candidates and politicos called out AI as one of the biggest issues in the blue wave, an important signpost ahead of a momentous 2028 presidential race.

  • Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), a 2028 contender who won reelection by a wide margin, called out "the titans of Silicon Valley" in a victory speech, saying they "dig bunkers for themselves" even as they warn "that the artificial intelligence they're creating risks human extinction."
  • AI had its "official debut" as the biggest issue in American politics, New York Assemblymember and RAISE Act author Alex Bores told Axios. "AI is reaching into every part of our society and economy, and it's now crystal clear it's impacting every part of our politics, too."

By the numbers: The anti-tech sentiment extended far beyond those states.

  • Out of 41 data center measures on the ballot across 10 states, about two dozen proposals designed to restrict or block development appeared to have passed based on initial returns, according to Ballotpedia.
  • Ohio hosted the largest share of those ballot fights, and some votes are still forthcoming, including in Arkansas and North Dakota.

Yes, but: In California, a measure that would've enacted a 5% wealth tax on individuals and trusts with more than $1 billion in assets appeared headed for defeat early Wednesday morning.

  • Proposition 40 faced a well-funded opposition from the state's tech luminaries, as well as prominent Democrats like Gov. Gavin Newsom and Xavier Becerra.

The intrigue: Leaning into AI skepticism proved to be a winning strategy for Democrats in swing districts.

  • Democratic challengers successfully weaponized AI policy, ousting Republicans in Ohio, Wisconsin, Arizona and Pennsylvania.
  • Democratic groups had poured ads into these districts attacking GOP incumbents for a 2025 vote that would've neutered state AI legislation.
  • AI safety advocates won or were poised to win races on Tuesday that will expand their coalition in the new Congress, including Colorado's Manny Rutinel and Minnesota's Matt Little.

The bottom line: For years, tech execs have dictated the terms of a seemingly limitless expansion, but this election proves that the ballot box still reigns supreme.

item.title: That dream job offer might be from a North Korean hacker
item.description:
North Korea appears to have used a fake job interview as part of its monthslong preparations to steal $6.3 billion from Binance, the crypto exchange said Tuesday.

Why it matters: The country's hackers are weaponizing both sides of the job market, posing as recruiters and job applicants to infiltrate companies and steal billions.

Driving the news: Binance said one of its software engineers was contacted in September through a "legitimate job-hunting platform" by someone posing as a project director at a fictitious company.

  • During the first-round interview, a fake HR representative conducted a live video call with the engineer and showed off a seemingly legitimate social media profile featuring personal photos and videos.
  • The hackers waited until the second round — after building trust with the employee — to ask them to download an infected code repository as part of an interview assignment.
  • Separately, another software engineer also downloaded a "tampered Homebrew installation" in June to install a popular AI coding tool onto their device. Binance's security team detected the installation and replaced the device, as well as rotated all credentials, but the engineer and colleagues were all exposed to the hacker.

The intrigue: The fake interview was just one of several suspected North Korean attempts to compromise Binance employees.

  • So far in 2026, Binance said it has detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber incidents, including attempts involving fake job interviews and compromised software packages.

Between the lines: North Korean hackers have spent years exploiting both sides of the hiring process.

  • As job applicants, North Korean operatives pose as legitimate IT workers to land high-paying jobs at American companies. Those salaries are then funneled back to Pyongyang.
  • Operatives are also increasingly posing as recruiters and prospective employees to lure in people who work at cryptocurrency firms in the hopes of tricking them into downloading malware.
  • Data from Pindrop Security shows that IT worker fraud has been rampant in 2026: Last year, North Korean job applicants made up 1 in every 343 applications. This year, across Pindrop's customer base, those applicants now make up 1 in 47.

The big picture: North Korea has found an opening in a difficult job market, where companies are eager to find qualified workers and job seekers are anxious for their next opportunity.

  • Hiring managers have struggled to find qualified candidates, while job applicants have been anxious for years about their ability to find new roles in a tough market.

Go deeper: How North Korea perfected the crypto heist

item.title: Prediction markets have a lot riding on the blue wave
item.description:
Prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket officially don't care which side of a bet wins.

  • There is no "house." They get their cut either way. It's a business model that's attracted billions of VC dollars.

Yes, but: Kalshi and Polymarket should be pulling hard for Democrats in today's midterm elections. Even if that feels counterintuitive.

Catch up quick: Prediction markets burst into the public consciousness two years ago, when their users correctly "picked" Donald Trump to beat Kamala Harris. It bestowed credibility at a time when public trust in traditional polling had cratered.

Fast forward: More recently, however, they had electoral misses in Brazil and Israel. Three would be a trend.

  • Both platforms currently have markets on Democrats sweeping Congress, with "yes" at around 75%.
  • If that's how today plays out, it would further cement prediction market legitimacy. A Republican win in either chamber, however, would dump them into the same pot as pollsters — even if 75% probability includes a sizable improbability.

Zoom in: Democrats are often more hostile to prediction markets than are Republicans, but companies like Kalshi and Polymarket don't have too much to fear from a Democrat-controlled Congress.

  • Yes, there would probably be an uncomfortable hearing or two. But neither chamber would have veto-proof majorities, and the Trump administration has been very sympathetic to the industry.
  • The real constraints, if any, are more likely to come via the Supreme Court.

The bottom line: Political predictions generate much less revenue for Kalshi and Polymarket than do sports predictions, but they have a much longer tail.

item.title: What we're watching on election night for energy
item.description:
There's a lot at stake for energy in the midterms, from the fate of the bipartisan permitting deal to the growing backlash against data centers and electricity prices.

Why it matters: The results could spotlight which energy topics resonate with voters — and which have become political liabilities.

  • Gasoline and diesel prices have been big on the campaign trail, offering a chance to see how much voter frustration over energy costs matters at the ballot box.

Data center politics: There are sharp differences between the parties, even though data centers aren't especially popular with either party's slate of candidates.

  • Why it matters: The pace of the AI buildout affects power demand and emissions.
  • State of play: 32.4% of Democratic candidates support moratoriums at the federal, state, or local level, compared to just 3.4% of Republicans, per Data Center Watch, which tracked hundreds of races.
  • Zoom in: Meanwhile, Ballotpedia is tracking dozens of ballot measures on data centers, many of which would impose new restrictions. Ohio is a hot spot.

Control and permitting: The outcome will affect the politics of the lame-duck session — and that means the politics of the bipartisan permitting deal.

  • What they're saying: If Democrats take both chambers, "leaders might opt to wait until they hold the gavels next year to renegotiate compromises," the research firm ClearView Energy Partners said in a note.
  • Yes, but: A reminder that backers of the current bill think it's folly to expect political space to write a more liberal bill that President Trump would sign, or that could even pass the Senate.
  • Threat level: What if the results are very close? ClearView notes that if Trump and allies contest the results, "weeks of post-election skirmishing could complicate passage of any bill."

Political lessons: The results could offer clues about where energy and climate policy are headed.

  • State of play: Exit polling is not famously precise, but it could provide a barometer of how much voters truly care — or not — about data centers.
  • It's also worth watching how candidates who made high gas and diesel prices central to their campaigns fare tonight.
  • My thought bubble: Keep an eye on the performance of progressive vs. centrist Democrats. If the latter overperform, it could be another sign that aggressive climate policies won't return to vogue with Dems.
  • Zoom in: Let's say, for instance, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro's (D) victory is even more of a blowout than expected. That could bolster more centrist, oil and gas-accepting candidates in the 2028 cycle (when he might run for president).

The next Congress: Regardless of chamber control, don't look for many opportunities for big new energy laws if permitting goes kaput.

  • Yes, but: There will be no shortage of messaging bills and positioning for the 2028 White House race. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) has pledged to bring back clean energy tax credits killed in the 2025 GOP budget law.
  • What we're watching: Limited chances for common ground around nuclear power and geothermal. For instance, the wide-ranging Senate permitting bill contains several bipartisan geothermal bills that already cleared the House.

Oversight power: If Democrats take control of either chamber, expect aggressive investigations of White House energy policies and investments, a topic we recently explored.

State utility bosses: A number of states have elections for electricity regulators, who often exert powerful control over power prices and planning.

  • Zoom in: One place to watch is Georgia, where two Democratic victories would flip party control of the state's Public Service Commission for the first time in decades. The Atlanta Journal-Constitution has more.

Governors: The winners of governors' races will have a big say in everything from oil and gas development to electricity prices.

  • Zoom out: S&P Global has a nice look at energy differences in several governors' races, though a number of the contests are not especially competitive.
  • Friction point: One place to watch is Texas, where oil and gas interests favor incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R) in his surprisingly tight race against Gina Hinojosa.

item.title: Three questions that will define AI's political power
item.description:
The 2026 midterms bring the first test of voter sentiment on the AI race, offering a window into how a niche policy debate is transforming into a wedge issue ahead of a presidential campaign cycle.

Why it matters: The results will reveal whether explicitly campaigning on AI regulation — or aligning with tech moguls like Elon Musk — is a winning political strategy or a liability for 2028.

  • One thing is already clear: Candidates increasingly can't afford to have half-baked AI agendas.

Here are three major questions about the future of AI politics and policy, and the races we're watching on Election Day for answers.

1. Did AI break through?

A different kind of AI political spending has emerged in the midterms. Instead of supporting or opposing candidates based on their AI positions, some groups want to make AI policy itself a campaign issue.

  • Guardrails Alliance, a pro-regulation advocacy group, recently launched ads targeting Republicans and Democrats over their positions on AI in Arizona, Montana, North Carolina and California.
  • The organization backed Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who said AI was the most important issue heading into Election Day, tying it explicitly to jobs and affordability.
  • Democratic group Tomorrow Together also launched ads against Republicans' AI track record in Michigan, Wisconsin, Arizona and Pennsylvania.
  • Meanwhile, competing AI groups Public First and Leading the Future spent more than $50 million through affiliated super PACs in nearly 50 races, but their TV and digital ads largely avoided the very issue they're trying to influence: AI.

These races could offer an early test of whether explicitly campaigning on AI is a viable political strategy heading into 2028.

2. Did Elon Musk help or hurt candidates?

Elon Musk's political spending, involvement in DOGE and ties to the Trump administration have made him both a powerful political backer and a target for Democratic attacks. He was the biggest donor in the midterms by far, contributing more than $400 million. Races we're watching include:

  • Texas' 10th District: Republican Chris Gober, who represented Musk in connection with DOGE, faces Democrat Caitlin Rourk.
  • Kansas' 1st District: Democrat Lauren Reinhold has leaned into her experience with DOGE, criticizing Musk's influence over the federal government in her challenge against Republican Rep. Tracey Mann.
  • Ohio Senate: Republican Jon Husted has benefited from spending by Musk's America PAC in his race against Democrat Sherrod Brown.
  • Texas Senate: Musk-affiliated spending has made the contest between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton another test of his political influence.

These races could help answer whether Musk's money helped elect Republican allies or gave Democrats a useful target.

3. How loud will the AI safety movement be in the next Congress?

A handful of candidates aligned with stronger AI safeguards could help determine whether the next Congress has a more vocal bloc pushing back against the industry's efforts to limit regulation. Races we're watching include:

  • Michigan Senate: El-Sayed wants a new Cabinet-level federal agency to regulate AI and a ban on superintelligence. He has used Musk's political involvement to attack Republican Mike Rogers, who has benefited from Musk-affiliated political spending.
  • Colorado's 8th District: Democrat Manny Rutinel sponsored the nation's first comprehensive AI bill.
  • California's 11th District: Democrat Scott Wiener's AI transparency legislation was at the center of a regulatory fight that divided the industry, offering a preview of battles in Washington.
  • Minnesota's 2nd District: Democrat Matt Little would add another voice to the push to ban data center construction and nondisclosure agreements at the national level.

These are some of the races that will help determine the size and influence of the AI safety movement's congressional coalition, an important indicator of where the fight over AI regulation is headed in 2027 and beyond.

The bottom line: Many factors will shape the outcomes of races across the country. But competing AI factions will be quick to claim victories, explain away losses and draw lessons about what worked ahead of 2028.

item.title: Elon Musk's next target: a major shake-up of America's wireless market
item.description:
Elon Musk is looking to shake up America's wireless industry, potentially bringing the first major new competitive threat in years to a business dominated by three companies.

Why it matters: The cellular industry has seen enormous technological change but relatively little disruption to its competitive structure. Musk has the money, spectrum and satellite network to attempt something different — though he faces daunting obstacles.

Driving the news: SpaceX is assembling the pieces to become a major U.S. wireless carrier, potentially building its own terrestrial network and buying available spectrum.

  • The moves are meant either to build the capability to bypass existing carriers or to bring them to the table for a deal that would allow Musk to strike a deal for wholesale access to their networks.
  • Musk may have reason to move quickly while the current administration and its regulatory appointees remain in place, a reason some analysts have cited in the context of proposals for a merger between Tesla and SpaceX.

What they're saying: Blair Levin, a former Federal Communications Commission chief of staff who now heads policy at Optimal Advisory, says Musk's financial resources distinguish him from previous challengers.

  • "For the first time, there is an entity capable of scaring investors in the traditional big three," Levin told Axios.
  • Unlike Dish, which faced serious financing constraints, SpaceX can draw on capital markets that have rewarded Musk's ambitious plans.

The latest: SpaceX has held talks with EchoStar about acquiring Boost Mobile or gaining access to its network arrangements, according to a Washington Post report Monday.

  • That could provide a quick route to customers and infrastructure, although approval of such a deal is far from a foregone conclusion if Musk's businesses are drawn into a regulator quagmire after the midterm elections.
  • The Post reported that Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile have all rebuffed Musk's efforts to gain access to their networks.

State of play: Musk also has a path to maneuver around them.

  • SpaceX has agreed to multibillion-dollar spectrum deals, including a low-band variety useful for reaching customers indoors and supporting a traditional cellular network.
  • The company could build its own network using towers and smaller rooftop antennas, though doing so would require substantial investment and time.

The big picture: America's wireless industry has spent much of the past two decades consolidating.

  • T-Mobile once played the scrappy challenger, shaking up the industry with aggressive pricing and the elimination of unpopular practices.
  • But its 2020 acquisition of Sprint reduced the number of major nationwide carriers from four to three.
  • Regulators tried to preserve a fourth competitor by requiring the sale of Boost Mobile to Dish Network, which planned to build a nationwide network.
  • That effort never delivered the competitive alternative envisioned, leaving Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile firmly entrenched.

The intrigue: Musk would be moving from a business where SpaceX enjoys enormous technical and economic advantages to one where the established players have spent decades building infrastructure, acquiring customers and learning how to serve them.

  • In terrestrial wireless, the big three carriers have invested in towers, spectrum, indoor coverage and the countless small improvements that make their networks reliable.
  • Building such a network isn't simply a matter of spending billions on infrastructure, Craig Moffett of MoffettNathanson said in a recent podcast interview. It also means catching up on decades of work filling in coverage gaps in stadiums, airports and other difficult locations.

The catch: Even if Musk can assemble the necessary infrastructure, it's far from clear that becoming a nationwide wireless carrier would be a particularly attractive business.

  • Moffett questions why SpaceX would want to enter an industry where even the established carriers struggle to earn attractive returns on their investments.

Between the lines: Success will depend on fundamentally lowering the cost of providing service or creating something for which consumers are willing to pay extra.

  • SpaceX has floated the idea of using Starlink rooftop equipment as small cellular base stations, potentially reducing some of the costs of building a traditional network.

The political backdrop: Musk's plans come as Washington faces a potentially significant shift following Tuesday's midterm elections.

  • While SpaceX is likely to face significant political and regulatory risks due to Musk's ties with Republicans, analysts aren't sure that will translate into opposing a wireless deal that adds competition to the market.

The bottom line: Musk has repeatedly succeeded in industries where established players doubted his ambitions. But this time he's the outsider, trying to overcome the advantages of companies that have spent decades building the networks he wants to challenge.

item.title: Europe's fridges are getting hacked. Could America be next?
item.description:
Cyberattacks are wreaking havoc on an unlikely target across Europe: supermarket refrigerators.

Why it matters: Hackers are turning everyday, internet-connected equipment into physical hazards, spoiling food and causing costly damage.

  • U.S. supermarkets use similar technology, and the Pentagon is already investigating suspected cyberattacks involving refrigeration systems at six military commissaries.

Driving the news: Suspected cyberattacks sent refrigerator and freezer temperatures soaring at dozens of European supermarkets overnight, spoiling food and threatening costly losses.

  • Grocery chains Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt reported incidents affecting stores in Belgium and Luxembourg, while Swedish chains ICA and Coop reported similar disruptions, per Reuters.
  • A Belgian company that operates Delhaize's refrigeration systems said hackers switched the units into defrost mode.

Here's what to know.

Supermarkets hacked in Europe

Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported cyberattacks or IT disruptions, forcing some stores to discard spoiled food.

  • Dozens of stores were affected, including an ICA supermarket in Sweden that said hackers set its refrigerator and freezer temperatures to 122°F, per ABC News.
  • Authorities haven't shared who specifically is behind the attacks, per NBC News.
Empty refrigerated shelves at a Proxy Delhaize supermarket in Maleizen, Belgium, following a refrigeration outage. Photo: Wiktor Dabkowski/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Flashback: The incidents follow similar attacks in France last month, when hackers seized control of hundreds of refrigeration units, causing fires and spoiling food. It's unclear whether the attacks are connected.

What they're saying: France's finance minister Roland Lescure said at the time that the attack "touches the heart of our food security."

  • "It was a wake-up call for everyone," he said.

How fridges get hacked

How it works: Hackers aren't opening up each individual fridge and setting new temperatures. Instead, they target computer systems that control the temperatures of multiple refrigerated units remotely.

  • Many stores use internet-connected controllers — small computer-like devices, sometimes with touchscreens — that allow maintenance workers to remotely monitor temperatures without having to visit every store.

Hackers can exploit software flaws or stolen login credentials to change temperatures or activate defrost functions.

Case in point: Danish manufacturer Danfoss said it identified security flaws last year and had long recommended customers install updates, according to The Guardian.

  • In the Netherlands, some affected refrigeration systems used default passwords and were connected to unsecured networks.
A supermarket manager discards spoiled food following a refrigeration outage linked to suspected cyberattacks across Europe on Nov. 2 in Belgium. Photo: Wiktor Dabkowski/Bloomberg via Getty Images

The cost of hacked refrigerators

  • Spoiled food: If temperatures rise overnight, the stores end up finding ruined meat, dairy and frozen products the next morning. In some French supermarkets, the soaring hot temperatures lasted for six hours, per Reuters. Spoiled food becomes unsafe to sell.
  • Overheating and fires: Refrigerators can also overheat and cause fires. French prosecutors confirmed that the October attacks caused fires and food losses.
  • Supermarkets lose money: Some stores lost more than €130,000. Two markets in the French region of Alsace reported combined losses of €270,000, per The Guardian. Intermarché's parent company estimated its nationwide losses in the tens of millions of euros.

Yes, but: Not every attack causes extensive damage. In Estonia, a refrigeration company said technicians responded to the breach within minutes and halted any massive losses, per AP.

Fridge attacks in the U.S.

Zoom out: Many U.S. supermarkets use refrigeration technology similar to that found in Europe.

  • Danfoss markets refrigeration monitoring and management systems in the U.S.
  • Copeland, a U.S.-based refrigeration technology company, sells controllers that manage the grocery store display cases and walk-in refrigerators.

What we're watching: The Pentagon is investigating whether cyberattacks caused freezer malfunctions at at least six U.S. military commissaries in August.

item.title: Pharma's next cash cows could be specialized treatments
item.description:
Pharmaceutical companies facing a steep patent cliff are concluding the key to future profits may be customized treatments tailored to patients' genes and lifestyles — not blockbusters aimed at large patient populations.

Why it matters: The pivot could influence which diseases get treated in the decades to come, and how much the health system pays.

  • The stakes are huge. More than $500 billion in brand-name drug sales is potentially at risk from generic competition between 2026 and 2032, according to the consulting firm Evaluate.

The latest: The race is on to find new treatments that each generate at least $2.4 billion in global sales, a new Iqvia Institute report finds.

  • They're increasingly specialty treatments, biologics and rare disease drugs — with a small group of flagship products accounting for an outsized share of industry sales.
  • GLP-1 drugs like Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Eli Lilly's Zepbound now define that elite category. The next wave could include "biological missiles" that combine antibodies with chemotherapy to target specific cancer cells.
  • "As precision medicine continues to advance, similar approaches may extend beyond oncology into areas such as immunology, metabolic disease and neurology," the report states.

Reality check: It's not clear whether all of the innovation will cure more people, or just make health care more expensive.

  • Novel RNA drugs and cell and gene therapies are expensive, hard to make and target small groups of patients.
  • Challenges identifying eligible patients and getting insurers to pay for treatments have already revealed a disconnect between promising R&D and patient benefit.
  • Widespread concern over high drug prices will force manufacturers to find more unmet needs and build sales more quickly after a drug's launch, according to the report.

Context: Top-selling drugs historically were aimed at large patient populations with chronic conditions like high cholesterol. The ulcer drug Tagamet became the first to exceed $1 billion in sales in 1986.

  • Over time, cancer and immunology drugs became major drivers of growth, followed by GLP-1s, which are sparking huge demand for conditions beyond obesity and diabetes but also driving up health costs.
  • Iqvia found that blockbusters on average maintain a dominant market position for 12.1 years before losing market exclusivity, or nearly 80% of their commercial life. Specialty drugs for rare or complex diseases lasted even longer.

Yes, but: A substantial number of top-sellers will lose patent protection and face potential competition from generics between 2028 and 2036.

  • Bristol Myers Squibb's blood thinner Eliquis and Merck's cancer blockbuster Keytruda, which are both due to lose market exclusivity in 2028, accounted for a combined $65 billion in global sales in 2024.

Follow the money: The search for new blockbusters is playing out in a highly charged environment. Drugmakers and biotechs not only have to figure out how to grow outside of crowded categories but also how much payers value new classes of drugs, Evaluate says.

  • There's also uncertainty over China, where Western drug giants have invested tens of billions of dollars to bolster their product pipelines.
  • Evaluate predicts that only autoimmune disease drugs will come close to rivaling GLP-1s, because of their potential to treat dozens of conditions.
  • One example is AbbVie's injectable Skyrizi for plaque psoriasis, arthritis, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, which could find more uses and generate more than $33 billion in sales in 2032.

Iqvia identifies RNA therapeutics as a potentially important middle ground between traditional "small molecule" drugs for chronic diseases and highly specialized genetic treatments.

  • These drugs can target disease-causing mutations across many genes and conditions, with applications for central nervous system, cardiovascular and kidney disease, as well as rare conditions.

The bottom line: The success at innovating while also making sure patients have access to the new treatments "will ultimately determine whether the growth in blockbuster medicines observed over the past 25 years can continue at its extraordinary pace," Iqvia concludes.

item.title: America's changing power grid faces a powerful El Niño
item.description:
A powerful El Niño could bring major shifts in electricity supply and demand across the U.S. this winter, posing new challenges for utilities.

Why it matters: The U.S. power grid has far more solar, wind and battery storage than during the last major El Niño, and the ongoing event could reveal whether that changing energy mix has made the grid more resilient or left it vulnerable in new ways.

Driving the news: A very strong El Niño is strengthening in the tropical Pacific and is expected to continue into spring 2027, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration says.

  • NOAA's latest outlook favors wetter-than-normal conditions across California, the Southwest and much of the southern U.S. this winter, while the northern Rockies and parts of the Great Lakes lean drier and much of the northern U.S. leans warmer.

The intrigue: El Niño doesn't affect every electricity resource the same way.

  • A March study found that previous super El Niños were associated with reductions in potential solar power output of nearly 5% in parts of California over 12 months — and more than 10% in the state's north during winter.
  • Vincent Tidwell, chief scientist at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, says a wetter California winter could boost hydropower, while reduced precipitation or snowpack in the Pacific Northwest could cut generation there.
  • Erik Smith, a climate scientist at the Electric Power Research Institute, tells Axios the Southeast is another region to watch for reduced solar generation as El Niño favors cloudier conditions.

California now has more than 21 gigawatts of battery capacity, giving the grid another tool to manage fluctuations in electricity supply — one it barely possessed during the last very strong El Niño.

  • The Columbia and Snake river basins accounted for roughly 62% of western U.S. hydropower generation between 2001 and 2020, according to a Pacific Northwest National Laboratory analysis.
  • Tidwell tells Axios that the Western grid is accustomed to shifting electricity between regions when hydropower conditions differ, helping compensate for shortages.
  • Federal water managers, states and utilities use seasonal forecasts to plan for potential hydropower availability at Hoover and Glen Canyon dams on the Colorado River, Tidwell says.

Zoom in: Tidwell expects natural gas to play a larger backup role if El Niño reduces Pacific Northwest hydropower and California solar generation this winter.

  • Other resources, including wind, geothermal and nuclear power, provide additional options, though he says El Niño's effects on wind generation remain poorly understood.

The big picture: A very strong El Niño could actually ease some pressure on the electricity system, Smith says.

  • Warmer-than-normal conditions across the northern U.S. could reduce winter heating demand, potentially offsetting some of the pressure from changing electricity supplies elsewhere.

Yes, but: Even a very strong El Niño doesn't guarantee specific weather effects.

  • A severe cold outbreak could still stress the grid despite a warmer-than-average winter, while a few major storms could radically alter regional rainfall and snowpack, Smith says.

The bottom line: "We have a lot of confidence in how the averages are going to play out, but we don't have a lot of confidence in the day-to-day, week-to-week, particular weather events that could drive those averages," Smith says.

item.title: I tested Apple's $2,000 iPhone Duo. It's a fascinating experiment, but the price is hard to justify.
item.description:
I've spent the past week trying to figure out whether Apple's $2,000 iPhone Duo is the future of smartphones or just an expensive way to do things I could already do on my regular iPhone.

  • The answer, unsurprisingly, is a bit of both.

Why it matters: Apple wasn't first to the folding smartphone party. Samsung, Google and others began making them years ago. But Apple's arrival in a category has a way of reinventing it.

The big picture: The most exciting thing about Apple's first foldable iPhone isn't necessarily what it can do today but what it can become. Already, it's inspiring developers to explore possibilities that could reshape how we use our devices.

Old habits die hard

One of my first surprises was how little I initially used the Duo's biggest selling point: its folding screen.

  • While other reviewers talked about endlessly opening and closing their devices, I found myself mostly using the smaller outside display. After years of conventional iPhones, it was a mix of instinct and muscle memory.

Zoom in: Over time, though, I found reasons to unfold it.

  • Watching sports was one of the clearest advantages. I pulled out the Duo at Starbucks to watch the 49ers with my son and later followed a tied World Series game in a doctor's waiting room.
  • At the WNBA Finals, having forgotten my laptop, I managed some quick edits to a story about Anthropic's IPO. I wouldn't want to write a full article that way, but it was reassuring to have the option.
  • Playing the New York Times' Spelling Bee alongside its Spelling Bee Buddy helper was a small but delightful example of multitasking without constantly switching apps.

Between the lines: The Duo's advantages aren't always about more screen space. Sometimes they're about what you can physically do with a phone that bends.

  • I tried watching Netflix with the phone unfolded, propped up like a tent and partially folded into a miniature laptop.
  • I also used the Duo's ability to stand on its own to capture wide shots of the WNBA Finals from a press-box ledge without needing a tripod.
  • Other experiences were less seamless, including getting the orientation right when trying FaceTime's option to use multiple camera views.

The developer wild card

Perhaps the biggest difference between the Duo and the Android foldables is the enthusiasm Apple's device has sparked among independent developers.

Zoom in: Some of the early experiments are more entertaining than useful, including apps that turn the Duo into a virtual cassette player or a grilled cheese toaster. My favorite was Tiny Computers, which let it simulate a semi-functional 1984 Mac, Windows 95 PC or candy-colored iMac.

  • Nearly two decades after the App Store debuted, we aren't all using our iPhones as virtual cigarette lighters. And I doubt we'll all be making imaginary grilled cheese sandwiches on our phones 20 years from now.

Zoom out: But these early experiments offer glimpses of what might be possible when developers start thinking beyond a conventional rectangular screen.

  • The question isn't whether today's novelties become hits. It's whether all this experimentation eventually produces genuinely new ways of using our phones — the kind of breakthroughs that make today's smartphones feel indispensable.

The $2,000 question

For all the fun I've had with the Duo, its price is an insurmountable obstacle. At $2,000, it's simply not a purchase I could justify for myself, much less recommend broadly.

The catch: There are other compromises. I missed Face ID, occasionally fumbling for the side-mounted Touch ID sensor until I started wearing an Apple Watch to make unlocking the phone easier. And when I needed to accomplish something quickly, I often instinctively reached for my familiar, traditional iPhone.

What I'm watching: On Friday, I tried putting the Duo away to see if I missed it. I didn't find myself longing for it the way I sometimes felt when I only had the Duo only and missed having a better camera.

The bottom line: The Duo is a fascinating glimpse of where smartphones could go next. But early buyers are paying a steep premium to participate in an experiment whose biggest rewards may still be years away.

item.title: Behind the Curtain: OpenAI's post-election power play
item.description:
Right after Tuesday's midterms, OpenAI will unleash a policy and PR blitz to try to get in sync with the new Washington, including an effort to rebrand data centers as "AI compute campuses."

Why it matters: After two years of a friendly White House, AI companies will face a harsher Washington after Tuesday, when Democrats will likely win the House. OpenAI also aims to help frame the AI debate for the big field of 2028 presidential contenders that'll start forming on Wednesday.

"You can try to chase the moment, or seek to inform the moment via the power of ideas," OpenAI chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane tells us, calling Tuesday an "electoral portal from one era to the next."

  • Since August, Lehane and his team have been stockpiling policy proposals, some new and some repackaged, to drive urgency and steer the AI debate.
  • It'll all start during the lame-duck session of Congress — the awkward but often consequential weeks between the election and the swearing-in of new members and senators on Jan. 3. This year's lame duck opens Nov. 9.

The big picture: Other tech companies are also positioning themselves for a potential blue wave. Meta is taking steps to strengthen its ties with Democrats, Axios' Sara Fischer scooped Saturday. Other big AI and tech players can be expected to do the same.

  • Tech titans who enjoy close relationships with President Trump will be top targets for Democrats, who are eager to ramp up scrutiny and regulatory pressure on the industry.

OpenAI's plans, being revealed here for the first time, all involve control — trying to send the message that AI is being built for people, not to displace people. The proposals include:

  1. Speed limits: Building on earlier proposals, OpenAI plans to unveil new ideas for mandatory safeguards for the most powerful AI systems — speed limits for AI that will allow humans to keep their hands on the wheel. This'll include a more aggressive congressional drive. "You're going to see us talk more and more about the concept of speed limits," Lehane said. "Our belief is people should always remain in control of this technology. AI should be built by and for people, and people should have more control over how the technology shapes their lives and communities."
  2. Data centers: OpenAI hopes to stem the nationwide, bipartisan backlash by offering new community compacts and commitments to smooth the way for future data centers. In addition, the company will try to set a new industry standard by proposing state legislation that gives people a meaningful say in how projects are built and what benefits they receive. In an intentionally provocative rebranding effort, OpenAI will argue that the infrastructure it's building, in contrast to legacy data centers, should be called "AI compute campuses" that can economically transform host communities. OpenAI points to its role in developing a huge data center project that promises to bring thousands of jobs to Pike County in Ohio's Appalachian region. "We think the conversation is good and healthy," Lehane said. "It's democracy in action. Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects."
